title: ‘Hormuz disruption driving structural shift in Middle East project logistics’
summary: Project owners are diversifying transport routes, building greater supply chain resilience and integrating logistics planning earlier in project development, says top Rhenus executive

Project owners are diversifying transport routes, building greater supply chain resilience and integrating logistics planning earlier in project development, says top Rhenus executive

Staff Writer ,  ZAWYA Projects

The disruption around the Strait of Hormuz is accelerating a structural shift in project cargo movements across the Middle East and Africa, according to a top executive of Germany-based global logistics company Rhenus Group.

Habeeb Kunhipurayil, Regional Head of Air & Ocean – Middle East at Rhenus Group, told Zawya Projects that companies are increasingly moving away from dependence on single shipping corridors as geopolitical uncertainty reshapes regional trade flows.

"The situation around the Strait of Hormuz is clearly changing how project cargo moves across the region," Kunhipurayil told Zawya Projects.

"We are seeing shifts in routing, pressure on traditional hubs, and a growing need to rethink how supply chains are structured. That said, this is not just about disruption. It is also pushing the industry to become more flexible and more resilient."

In response to the changing operating environment, Rhenus has activated a new Europe-Middle East multimodal corridor linking Türkiye and Europe with the Gulf via Jordan.

According to the company, more than 190 tonnes of cargo were transported through the route during its first month of operations. The corridor was tested through an 18-day multimodal shipment of oilfield equipment from Lyon to Dubai, including cross-stuffing operations in Jordan to comply with GCC transport requirements.

"For us, the priority was to act quickly and stay close to our customers," Kunhipurayil said.

"We moved fast to establish a multimodal corridor between Europe and the Middle East, combining road and short-sea transport. It provides customers with a reliable alternative while reducing dependence on the most exposed routes."

He said the company is also leveraging its global logistics network and container capabilities to route cargo through multiple gateways as shipping patterns evolve.

“It is about being practical and finding solutions that work in the real world,” he said.

Capacity and planning challenges

Despite the alternative routes, Kunhipurayil acknowledged that project logistics remain challenging, with tighter transport capacity, less predictable shipping schedules and increased cross-border coordination requirements.

"The environment is not straightforward, but this is exactly where experience counts," he said. "Our teams are accustomed to managing complexity, and we rely on close communication with customers and partners to keep cargo moving."

Looking ahead, the Rhenus Group executive expects market volatility to persist but believes logistics resilience will increasingly depend on preparation rather than prediction.

"We have a diversified network, multiple transport options and strong local teams on the ground," he said. "It is less about predicting every scenario and more about being ready to respond quickly and effectively when conditions change."

Kunhipurayil said the current market reinforces the need for project developers to integrate logistics considerations much earlier in project planning.

"In the current environment, timelines and costs are no longer as predictable as they once were, so building flexibility into projects from the outset is essential," he said.

"Choosing the right logistics partner makes a real difference. With the right support, even complex situations like this can be managed with confidence," he concluded.

(Reporting by Dennis Daniel; Editing by Anoop Menon)
